newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: US study says enough evidence to convict Khmer Rouge chiefs.
newsitem.headline: US study says enough evidence to convict Khmer Rouge chiefs.

text.p: The U.S.-funded Cambodian Genocide Programme has discovered enough new evidence to convict Khmer Rouge leaders of crimes against humanity during their brutal 1975-79 rule, a local newspaper reported on Saturday
"The entire DK (Khmer Rouge) leadership is implicated," the fortnightly Phnom Penh Post quoted Craig Etcheson of Yale University's Cambodian Genocide Programme (CGP) as saying.

Etcheson, who could not be reached at his office in the United States on Saturday, said the mass of information collected over the past two years was sufficient to convict them of crimes against humanity if they were ever brought to trial.

The evidence, including gravesites, signed execution orders, documents on workings of the Khmer Rouge security service, was significant because of "the extent to which it reveals centralised control of the killing in DK."
He mentioned no names but several top leaders of the "killing fields" regime are known or believed to still be alive and in territory controlled by Khmer Rouge hardliners.
They include Pol Pot, the leader of the group, his deputy Nuon Chea, nominal Khmer Rouge leader Khieu Samphan, defence chief Son Sen and feared one-legged commander Ta Mok.

Former Khmer Rouge foreign minister Ieng Sary joined the government last year after receiving a royal amnesty from a 1979 death sentence handed down in absentia for his role in the deaths of more than one million people under the Pol Pot regime.
Cambodia's King Norodom Sinhanouk pardoned Ieng Sary after the country's two premiers asked him to do in the interests of national reconciliation.

The U.S. State Department in 1994 gave $500,000 to the Yale team to gather evidence of human rights abuses by the Pol Pot regime. The CGP has used up the grant but recently received support from other sources for two more years of research.
The United States has said a decision on whether or not to go ahead with a trial, international or domestic, was left to the Cambodian people.

Cambodian government views on the top Khmer Rouge leaders have softened since Ieng Sary's August split with the hardliners encouraged thousands of rebels join the government, but officials say Pol Pot can never be forgiven.
